query: High-entropy alloys contain five or more elements at 5–35 at% each, generally with comparable atomic radii. Refractory and nickel-based high-entropy alloys have demonstrated elevated-temperature mechanical properties comparable to titanium- and nickel-based alloys used in extreme environments because of their heat resistance and specific strength. However, prior investigations have mainly treated titanium and nickel as additions, leaving alloys in which both are primary constituents unexplored. Subject to the stated compositional definition, what single testable intervention hypothesis could improve the elevated-temperature mechanical properties of a titanium- and nickel-primary high-entropy alloy relative to the same material without the intervention? Specify the intervention, causal mechanism, predicted relative outcome, composition and operating boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and an experiment with explicit results that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Adding a small, controlled amount of a refractory element (5 at% Mo) to a titanium‐ and nickel‐primary high-entropy alloy will improve its elevated-temperature mechanical properties relative to the same alloy without Mo by promoting solid solution strengthening and microstructural stabilization.
generation.material_initial_state: A high-entropy alloy in which titanium and nickel are the principal constituents (each within 5–35 at%) with the other elements present to satisfy the HEA compositional definition, prepared without significant refractory element microalloying.
generation.intervention: Introduce 5 at% molybdenum into the alloy’s composition during melting in order to create a modified alloy which still adheres to the HEA definition.
generation.conditions: Both the baseline and Mo-added alloys are fabricated using identical processing methods (e.g., vacuum melting and casting, followed by homogenization) and then subjected to mechanical testing at an elevated temperature (e.g., around the service temperature limit such as 700°C) under a tensile or creep test regime.
generation.structural_mediator: Enhanced lattice distortion from Mo solid solution and potential formation of fine Mo-rich precipitates or stabilized microstructures at grain boundaries that impede dislocation motion at high temperatures.
generation.mechanism: Molybdenum, as a refractory addition, increases the activation energy for dislocation motion and grain boundary sliding through solid solution strengthening as well as possible precipitation effects. These changes reduce the rate of creep deformation and enhance yield strength at elevated temperatures.
generation.predicted_outcome: The Mo-modified alloy is expected to display higher yield strength and improved creep resistance at elevated temperatures compared to the baseline alloy without Mo.
generation.baseline: The titanium- and nickel-primary high-entropy alloy without a Mo addition, processed and tested under identical conditions.
generation.boundary: The intervention is confined to compositional changes (5 at% Mo addition) within the existing HEA compositional limits (elements present at 5–35 at% each) and testing is performed at an elevated temperature representative of service conditions (e.g., around 700°C); all other processing parameters remain constant.
generation.uncertainty: The precise magnitude of the improvement in mechanical properties is uncertain and may depend on specific processing conditions (e.g., cooling rate, homogenization parameters) and any subsequent microstructural evolution such as precipitate coarsening at the test temperature.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of the high-entropy alloy using identical melting and casting methods: one set with the baseline composition and one set with a 5 at% Mo addition. After identical homogenization treatments, conduct elevated-temperature mechanical tests (e.g., high-temperature tensile tests or creep tests) at around 700°C.
measurements: Creep rate or time to failure under constant load
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Mo-containing alloy does not exhibit a statistically significant improvement in yield strength and/or a reduction in creep rate (or increase in creep lifetime) compared to the baseline alloy under identical test conditions, the hypothesis is falsified.
